credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A Texas-sized iron asteroid is knocked out of the asteroid belt toward Earth by a comet collision.
critique: No asteroid that big exists (Ceres is ~900 km, Texas ~1400 km) and a comet could not shove a ~5e24 g iron body out of its orbit: 'you could ram it with comets for years and not move it much.'
status_reason: Ceres (~940 km) remains the largest main-belt body; momentum conservation makes a comet impact negligible for such a mass.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The 'Texas-sized' asteroid is jagged and spiky.
critique: A body that large is pulled into a sphere by its own gravity; a collision big enough to send it to Earth would have melted it round.
status_reason: Bodies above a few hundred km (e.g. Ceres, Vesta near the limit) approach hydrostatic shapes; a 1000+ km body would be near-spherical, as Dawn confirmed for Ceres.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The cosmonaut spins the Russian space station to create gravity just before the shuttles dock.
critique: A spinning station would be very hard to dock with, the small docking tube couldn't hold the shuttle against spin 'gravity', and the movie's 'gravity goes every which way'; at the hub there would be no force at all.
status_reason: Centripetal pseudo-gravity points outward from the spin axis and vanishes at the hub; docking with a spinning body requires matching rotation.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A nuclear bomb splits the 1000-km asteroid four hours before impact so both halves miss Earth.
critique: Each half would need ~1600 km/h sideways in 4 hours; for that mass this needs ~1e11 megatons, roughly the Sun's output per second - 'one bomb ain't gonna do it. A billion or so might.'
status_reason: Simple kinetic-energy arithmetic; modern deflection studies (and NASA's 2022 DART test) emphasize years of lead time, not last-hour splitting.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: On the asteroid, crew need thrusters to stay on the surface, yet inside the ship they walk normally.
critique: 'The writers forgot that gravity can penetrate even the impenetrable titanium of the rocket's hull' - the pilot running inside should have launched herself into the walls.
status_reason: Gravity cannot be shielded; the low surface gravity applies inside the lander too.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Astronauts walk and bounce on the 11-km comet as if in moderate gravity.
critique: An 11-km comet has surface gravity ~1/10,000 of Earth's and escape velocity of a few m/s - an 80 kg astronaut would weigh ~12 g and could easily leap off.
status_reason: Rosetta's Philae bounce on 67P (2014, escape speed ~1 m/s) dramatically confirmed how feeble comet gravity is.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The comet surface is shown bright white/gray.
critique: Comets are among the darkest objects in the solar system; Giotto found Halley's nucleus 'darker than coal', reflecting ~3-4% of light.
status_reason: Later missions (Deep Impact/Tempel 1, Rosetta/67P with ~6% albedo) confirmed very dark nuclei.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Before the tsunami hits, the water near the beach recedes dramatically.
critique: Because the impact wave travels faster than sound, distant water would have 'no warning' and should not recede before the wave arrives (Plait later added a hedge after reader corrections).
status_reason: Drawdown happens whenever a wave trough arrives first (as seen in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami); impact-generated tsunamis are wave trains, so recession before a crest is plausible.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Astronauts blow up the second comet fragment minutes before impact, saving Earth.
critique: 'Blowing up a comet does no good at all' - if the pieces still hit, all the kinetic energy is still dumped into the atmosphere, dwarfing all nuclear arsenals combined.
status_reason: Correct for a last-minute disruption, but recent planetary-defense work (e.g. 'pulverize it' fragmentation studies, 2020s) finds that breaking a body into small pieces with adequate lead time can spread energy so it is largely harmless.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: When the Machine activates its strong gravity field, ships in the harbor lean toward it.
critique: Buoyancy keeps decks perpendicular to local gravity, so the ships should heel the other way, decks tilting away from the Machine (point credited to a reader, added 2001).
status_reason: A floating hull aligns its deck with the local equipotential surface, i.e. normal to the net gravity vector.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Ellie experiences ~18 hours in transit while zero time passes on Earth.
critique: Even moving at relativistic or superluminal speed, her conversation with her 'father' takes time, so some time must elapse in Earth's frame; a zero-time trip 'won't work' without alien time manipulation.
status_reason: Sound in principle (any nonzero proper time maps to nonzero external time along ordinary paths), but wormhole geometries can act as time machines (Morris-Thorne-Yurtsever 1988), so zero elapsed Earth time is exotic rather than strictly impossible.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
depiction: Ships are silhouetted against sunlit Naboo with a sky full of bright stars.
critique: Contrast: a sunlit planet is thousands of times brighter than stars, so any exposure showing the planet properly would show no stars - you never see stars in shuttle footage of Earth.
status_reason: Dynamic-range limits of eyes and cameras; ISS imagery still shows the same effect.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
depiction: Tatooine orbits two suns of similar apparent size that set together.
critique: Analyzes binary-star orbits: figure-8 orbits are unstable, an S-type orbit would make the far star look small, so the likely configuration is a stable circumbinary (P-type) orbit far outside both stars; also notes scenes show single shadows.
status_reason: Kepler-16b (2011) and later circumbinary planets (Kepler-34b, -35b, TOI-1338b) confirmed exactly the stable P-type 'Tatooine' configuration he favored.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
depiction: Padme tells Anakin 'space is cold'.
critique: Space itself has no temperature; a thermometer in space reads whatever radiation it absorbs - hot near a star, ~3 K far from any star because of the cosmic background.
status_reason: Equilibrium temperature depends on radiative balance; CMB at 2.725 K sets the floor.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
depiction: Obi-Wan dogfights through Geonosis's dense ring of huge tumbling boulders.
critique: Real ring particles (Saturn's) are at most a few meters; such a dense field of big rocks would grind itself to dust by collisions long ago.
status_reason: Cassini (2004-2017) confirmed Saturn's ring particles are mostly cm-to-m sized with sparse spacing; collisional grinding limits sizes.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
depiction: Jango Fett's seismic charges produce a booming shock wave in space.
critique: Sound needs a medium; in vacuum there would be no sound and no blast wave.
status_reason: No acoustic propagation in vacuum; debris ring gas is far too thin.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
depiction: Count Dooku flies a solar-sail ship to a distant star system.
critique: Light pressure gives tiny accelerations; sails are fine for interplanetary travel but crossing 'halfway across the galaxy' by sail would take thousands to hundreds of thousands of years.
status_reason: IKAROS (2010) and LightSail 2 (2019) confirmed micro-newton-scale thrust; interstellar sails need laser beaming (e.g. Breakthrough Starshot concept).

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith
depiction: After the cruiser loses artificial gravity, the corridor tilts and people slide down the floor as it falls toward the planet.
critique: Falling under the planet's gravity, everything aboard accelerates equally, so without artificial gravity they should float, not slide - which is why orbiting astronauts float.
status_reason: Equivalence principle: free-falling objects share the same acceleration (atmospheric drag later would add some deceleration).

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
work: Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith
depiction: The falling cruiser burns as it re-enters the atmosphere.
critique: Points out re-entry heating is not mainly friction but compression of the air ahead of the ship (ram/shock heating).
status_reason: Re-entry heating is dominated by shock-layer compression of gas ahead of the vehicle, with friction a minor contributor.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: An astronaut takes off his helmet in space and instantly freezes solid, his face distorting.
critique: The body holds lots of heat and in vacuum can lose it only by slow radiation, so he would not freeze quickly; nor would he explode.
status_reason: Vacuum-exposure data (e.g. 1966 NASA chamber accident) show unconsciousness in ~15 s but no instant freezing or explosion.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Dr Pepper leaking through a meteoroid hole freezes in place almost instantly outside the hull.
critique: The liquid wouldn't freeze so quickly: in vacuum heat can only be radiated away, 'a very inefficient and slow process.'
status_reason: Liquid exposed to vacuum flash-boils and evaporative cooling freezes the remainder within seconds (as with shuttle/ISS water dumps forming ice crystals), so rapid freezing is realistic.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Terri Fisher fires her suit jets for a long time chasing her husband, then gives only a brief burst to stop.
critique: No friction in space: Newton's laws mean she must spend as much thrust stopping as she spent accelerating, so a short burst could not stop her.
status_reason: Delta-v to stop equals delta-v gained; elementary Newtonian mechanics.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: When power returns, the ship's spin wheels restore gravity instantly and everything drops to the floor.
critique: Spin gravity can't switch on like a light: the wheels must spin up gradually, and objects floating inside wouldn't immediately 'fall' until the moving floor reaches them.
status_reason: Centripetal pseudo-gravity scales with spin rate and only acts on objects co-rotating with the structure.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The ship uses two counter-rotating gravity wheels; a fire extinguisher's spray pushes Bowman backwards.
critique: Praises both: counter-rotating wheels cancel angular momentum so the ship itself doesn't spin, and extinguisher recoil in weightlessness is accurate.
status_reason: Angular momentum and momentum conservation, standard design practice for spin habitats.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Astronauts on Mars stand against a pinkish-orange sky.
critique: Close: suspended dust makes the Martian daytime sky 'butterscotch' rather than blue, as seen by Viking and Pathfinder.
status_reason: Curiosity and Perseverance imagery confirm a butterscotch daytime sky with blue sunsets from dust forward-scattering.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Earth's magnetic field fails because the iron core stopped rotating.
critique: Stopping the core would require removing ~1e35 erg of rotational energy, the Sun's output for ~100 s or five trillion one-megaton bombs - 'just plain old silly.'
status_reason: The geodynamo is driven by convection in the liquid outer core; even 2023 seismic hints that the inner core's rotation relative to the mantle paused involve tiny differential motions, not a halt.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Without the magnetic field, deadly cosmic rays and microwave beams from space strike Earth (one cuts the Golden Gate Bridge).
critique: The magnetic field deflects some charged cosmic rays, but the atmosphere blocks most of them; a weakened field would not be deadly, and there are no natural space microwave beams to slice bridges.
status_reason: Paleomagnetic records show past geomagnetic reversals/excursions (e.g. Laschamp, ~41 ka) caused no mass extinctions; the atmosphere provides ~10 m water-equivalent shielding.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Krypton's red giant sun collapses and explodes as a supernova, tearing the planet apart.
critique: A Sun-like red giant sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf; it does not explode. (Comic canon also has the planet, not the star, exploding.)
status_reason: Only stars above ~8 solar masses (red supergiants) undergo core-collapse supernovae; low-mass red giants end as planetary nebulae and white dwarfs.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Superman hovers motionless above the atmosphere, cape flapping, hearing a cry for help.
critique: No sound in space - and his cape shouldn't flap since he isn't moving and there's no air.
status_reason: No medium for sound or air drag above the atmosphere.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A NASA engineer says you need only hit a baseball halfway to the Moon and the Moon's gravity takes over.
critique: The Moon has ~1/80 Earth's mass, so at the halfway point Earth's pull is still ~80 times stronger; the balance point is about 90% of the way to the Moon.
status_reason: Gravitational balance point ~346,000 km from Earth (~0.9 of the distance).

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The engineer says jumping on a trampoline in space would make you go 'up and up and up'.
critique: You can't really bounce on a trampoline in weightlessness: push off once and you just drift away, as from a wall, with nothing to bring you back.
status_reason: Without a restoring force (gravity) there is no oscillating bounce.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Giant robots that crater the ground transform into ordinary-weight cars; the huge AllSpark cube shrinks to hand size.
critique: Shrinking an object doesn't change its mass: a 10-20 ton robot folded into a car would be incredibly dense and heavy - 'Drive over a bridge and see what happens!'
status_reason: Conservation of mass; density scales inversely with volume.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: An official says Earth's gravitational field at the North Pole scrambled Megatron's navigation.
critique: The line clearly means the magnetic field; sci-fi constantly confuses gravity with magnetism.
status_reason: Gravity is nearly uniform with latitude; it is the geomagnetic field that disturbs compasses near the poles.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Alien beam weapons blow planets into giant pieces in the opening montage.
critique: It's really hard to blow up a planet: each piece must be given escape velocity (~11 km/s for Earth), an enormous gravitational binding energy.
status_reason: Earth's gravitational binding energy is ~2e32 J, about a week of the Sun's total output.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A crewman sucked out through a hull breach is implied to suffer boiling blood.
critique: 'To the immediate point about blood boiling, it wouldn't happen' - the circulatory system keeps blood pressurized above vapor pressure.
status_reason: Blood pressure keeps blood liquid in vacuum; only saliva/tears and tissue water (ebullism swelling) vaporize, per decompression-accident data.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Nero's mining drill bores a hole to Vulcan's core to drop red matter in.
critique: Rock pressure would collapse the borehole and the plastic mantle would flow in: 'the pressure of the overlying rocks tends to collapse the hole.'
status_reason: The deepest real borehole (Kola, 12 km) stalled because of heat and rock plasticity; a hole thousands of km deep is impossible.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A drop of red matter turns Vulcan into a black hole that swallows the planet and endangers ships in orbit.
critique: Making a black hole takes a lot of mass, infalling matter would blaze in X-rays, and once Vulcan collapsed 'the gravity felt by the orbiting ships didn't change!'
status_reason: Outside a spherically symmetric mass, gravity depends only on enclosed mass (Birkhoff's theorem); a planet-mass black hole pulls no harder on orbiting ships.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: From Delta Vega, Spock watches Vulcan's destruction looming huge in the sky.
critique: For Vulcan to look that big, Delta Vega must be only a few hundred thousand km away at most - i.e. effectively a close moon of Vulcan (and he questions why an outpost would be there).
status_reason: Angular size = diameter/distance; a planet subtending tens of degrees must be within roughly a few planetary radii to a few hundred thousand km.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A supernova threatens to destroy the whole galaxy and Romulus.
critique: Supernovae can only physically hurt planets within about 50 light-years; threatening the galaxy is absurd. Also 'as far as we know, yellow stars can't blow.'
status_reason: The 'kill radius' estimate (~25-50 ly for ozone damage) still stands, and Sun-like single stars do not explode, but white dwarfs in binaries do (Type Ia), so 'yellow' systems are not fully immune.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Red-matter black hole is used to 'consume' the supernova and stop it.
critique: A black hole wouldn't stop a supernova - core-collapse supernovae can already form black holes at their centers.
status_reason: Core collapse itself forms neutron stars/black holes; the expanding ejecta would not be swallowed by a small central black hole.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Nero's ship and the Jellyfish are drawn into a black hole and the Enterprise escapes intact.
critique: Tidal forces near a small black hole would rip the ship apart (spaghettification): 'The difference in gravity between your feet and head could be millions of times the Earth's gravity!'
status_reason: Tidal acceleration ~2GM L/r^3 is enormous near a low-mass black hole's horizon.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The Enterprise ejects its warp core and is pushed away by the explosion's shock wave.
critique: In vacuum there is no air to carry a shock wave; momentum transfer from expanding debris/radiation 'would be minimal'.
status_reason: There is no air blast in space, but a very energetic explosion's debris and plasma could still impart momentum at close range, so the push is not strictly impossible.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Using a jetpack (MMU), Clooney and Bullock travel from Hubble to the ISS.
critique: Hubble orbits ~110 m/s slower than the ISS and in an orbit 'tipped at wildly different angles'; the MMU can only deliver ~25 m/s, so the transfer is impossible.
status_reason: Plane changes between 28.5 deg and 51.6 deg inclinations need km/s of delta-v; no crewed jetpack can do it.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Clooney, tethered and stopped relative to the ISS, drifts away and must let go to save Bullock.
critique: Once they stopped they were in free fall with no net force; 'literally an ounce of force applied for a few seconds would've been enough' to pull him back.
status_reason: Same point as Tyson; with zero relative velocity there is no tension pulling him away (only minor tidal/rotational effects).

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Bullock uses a fire extinguisher as a thruster to reach Tiangong.
critique: Probably impossible: thrusting with an extinguisher not aligned through her center of mass would send her tumbling; and Tiangong's orbit is inclined ~10 deg from the ISS so a Soyuz couldn't easily match it either.
status_reason: Off-axis thrust produces torque; plane changes are expensive in delta-v.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Shuttle crew killed by debris are shown frozen almost immediately.
critique: Freezing bodies in vacuum would take hours, since heat leaves only by radiation (and slow evaporation).
status_reason: Radiative cooling of a human-mass body takes many hours; vacuum is an insulator.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Debris from a destroyed satellite returns every ~90 minutes to hit Hubble, the shuttle and the ISS.
critique: Debris stays in roughly its parent's orbit, so it could only hit Hubble and ISS if satellite orbits intersected theirs, which operators avoid; debris would not sweep all altitudes and inclinations together.
status_reason: Fragment clouds spread along the parent orbit (seen after the 2007 Fengyun-1C and 2021 Kosmos-1408 ASAT tests) rather than covering all altitudes.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Miller's planet orbits Gargantua so close that one hour there equals seven years on Earth (~60,000x time dilation).
critique: Such dilation requires skimming the horizon, but 'the minimum stable orbit around a black hole must be at least three times the size of the black hole itself,' so the planet would fall in.
status_reason: Plait retracted it two days later: for a near-maximally spinning Kerr black hole (as Kip Thorne specified) stable orbits exist close enough for that dilation; he wrote the film's time dilation 'was in fact accurate.' (source of retraction: https://www.syfy.com/syfy-wire/follow-interstellar-mea-culpa)

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Giant mountain-high waves roll across the shallow seas of Miller's planet.
critique: Kept after his mea culpa: he still objects to the giant 'tidal waves', arguing such a planet's tides and shallow seas could not produce them.
status_reason: A perfectly locked planet would have static tides, but Thorne's explanation (a slight rocking libration producing periodic tidal bores) is physically plausible; the critique holds only for an exactly locked orbit.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Planets around Gargantua are lit and warmed although there is no star nearby; the accretion disk looks calm and dim.
critique: 'Where do the planets get heat and light?' The disk isn't bright enough to light and heat the planets; a real disk would be extremely hot and fast-moving, and planets would be pelted by infalling matter.
status_reason: Thorne deliberately chose an unusually cold, quiescent disk, which is then too dim to warm planets as Plait says; but a brighter disk would irradiate them with X-rays, so the scenario is internally strained rather than simply wrong.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: The Enterprise whooshes audibly past the camera in space.
critique: 'Well, it's Trek. That means we hear sounds in space' - sound needs a medium; even a nebula's gas could not carry sound as we know it, and computer-added-sound retcons don't explain what outside viewers hear.
status_reason: No acoustic propagation in vacuum; interstellar gas densities (~1 atom/cm^3) cannot carry audible sound.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: At warp 4.5 the ship reaches Neptune and back in six minutes, yet the Klingon homeworld is 'four days' away.
critique: Six minutes to Neptune and back is ~80c; four days at 80c is under one light-year - closer than the nearest star, Proxima Centauri (~20 days' travel at that speed).
status_reason: Proxima Centauri at 4.24 ly remains the nearest star; simple distance/speed arithmetic.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Stars stream rapidly past the windows during warp.
critique: If the nearest star takes ~20 days to reach, roughly one star should flash by every ~20 days on average; the streaks can't be dust because they resolve into stars when the ship drops out of warp.
status_reason: Mean interstellar spacing (~5 ly locally) means stars pass very rarely even at 80c.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A comet cruises through an asteroid belt crowded with hundreds of visible rocks and smashes into two of them.
critique: Even in the thickest part of the belt, asteroids are typically millions of miles apart; a comet hitting even one is unlikely, two essentially impossible.
status_reason: Spacecraft (Pioneer, Galileo, Dawn, Lucy) cross the belt without special avoidance; mean separations are ~1e6 km.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: A small fragment hits Montana days before the main asteroids arrive.
critique: Fragments knocked onto the new orbit stay on that orbit and travel with the main body; they would not arrive days ahead.
status_reason: Small velocity dispersions from a collision spread fragments only slowly along the orbit, as seen in asteroid families and DART/Dimorphos ejecta.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Two airborne lasers are used to destroy a 10-km asteroid.
critique: A 10-km rock is the size of a large mountain, ~a trillion tons; 'picture two lasers on board an aircraft trying to vaporize Mt. Everest.'
status_reason: Megawatt-class airborne lasers (the cancelled YAL-1 program) deliver far too little energy to vaporize a mountain-sized body.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: An iron asteroid ~10x5x3 km at 50,000 mph is said to hit with the force of 30 atomic bombs.
critique: An iron body that size at that speed would release vastly more energy than 30 atomic bombs - the line 'made me laugh out loud'.
status_reason: KE ~ 0.5 x 1.2e15 kg x (22 km/s)^2 ~ 3e23 J, about 70 million megatons.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Nineteen minutes before impact, the incoming asteroid is shown passing over the Moon.
critique: The Moon is ~250,000 miles away, five hours at 50,000 mph; 19 minutes out the rock would be only ~17,000 miles away, closer than geosynchronous satellites.
status_reason: Simple distance/speed arithmetic.

credentials: PhD astronomy (University of Virginia, 1994); former Hubble Space Telescope (STIS) team astronomer; Bad Astronomy author
depiction: Two nuclear missiles blow up the iron asteroid.
critique: The asteroid is roughly the volume of Mt. Everest and solid iron; two atomic bombs 'would not do a whole lot of damage' and certainly wouldn't vaporize it.
status_reason: Two small fission bombs indeed could not vaporize it, but standoff-burst studies (e.g. the 2024 Sandia Z-machine X-ray ablation experiment in Nature Physics) show nuclear X-ray pulses can usefully deflect km-scale bodies, so nukes are not useless if the goal is deflection.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: The spaceship plunges into a black hole whose interior looks like a cave with fiery stalactites and stalagmites.
critique: Essay 'Hollywood Nights': the film ignores what really happens near a black hole - tidal forces that would stretch the ship apart, time dilation, jets - instead showing a 'dank cave'.
status_reason: General relativity predicts spaghettification for stellar-mass holes and extreme time dilation near the horizon; EHT images (2019, 2022) show luminous accretion flows, not caverns.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Ellie says if one in a million stars has planets, one in a million of those has life, and one in a million of those intelligent life, there would be millions of civilizations.
critique: Her own arithmetic gives 400 billion x 1e-18 = '0.0000004 planets with intelligent life on them,' not millions.
status_reason: The arithmetic is correct; moreover Kepler/TESS results show most stars host planets, so the movie's 'one in a million have planets' factor is also far too pessimistic.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Hours on Miller's planet near the black hole Gargantua equal years on Earth.
critique: Strong gravity really slows time ('is real, by the way'); an extreme case is plausible because 'they made it clear this is a planet orbiting a black hole.'
status_reason: Gravitational time dilation is measured daily (GPS) and the ~60,000x factor is attainable near a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole (Thorne 2014).

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: The crew travels to another galaxy through a wormhole near Saturn.
critique: Wormhole math and physics are sound, 'but we don't know how to make one, and even if we did make one, the equations show that they're unstable.'
status_reason: Traversable wormholes still require exotic negative-energy matter to stay open; no mechanism is known as of 2026.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: The Moon is revealed to be a hollow artificial megastructure knocked from its orbit toward Earth.
critique: Said Moonfall dethroned Armageddon as the biggest violator of physical laws, mocking the hollow Moon containing a giant built structure.
status_reason: Apollo seismometers, the Moon's moment of inertia (0.393) and GRAIL gravity mapping show a solid, differentiated body with a small dense core - not hollow.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Debris from a destroyed satellite sweeps around Earth and strikes the shuttle, Hubble and ISS.
critique: Tweet: 'Nearly all satellites orbit Earth west to east yet all satellite debris portrayed orbited east to west' - debris should share the prograde motion of its parent satellites.
status_reason: Almost all satellites are launched prograde to use Earth's rotation; fragments keep roughly their parent's orbit, so retrograde debris streams are implausible.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Sandra Bullock's hair stays neatly in place during otherwise convincing weightless scenes.
critique: Tweet: 'Why Bullock's hair, in otherwise convincing zero-G scenes, did not float freely on her head.'
status_reason: In free fall hair has no weight to pull it down and drifts freely, as ISS footage shows.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: After Clooney releases Bullock's tether he drifts away to his death as if pulled.
critique: Tweet: 'When Clooney releases Bullock's tether, he drifts away. In zero-G a single tug brings them together.'
status_reason: Once the pair's motion relative to the station has stopped there is no net force pulling Clooney away; a gentle tug would bring him back (residual rotation could add only a small tension).

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Hubble, the ISS and a Chinese space station are close enough to see and reach from one another.
critique: Tweet: 'How Hubble (350mi up) ISS (230mi up) & a Chinese Space Station are all in sight lines of one another.'
status_reason: Hubble (~540 km, 28.5 deg) and ISS (~420 km, 51.6 deg) are at different altitudes and inclinations and are generally thousands of km apart.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: A chain reaction of debris collisions destroys satellites across low Earth orbit.
critique: Tweet: 'The film #Gravity depicts a scenario of catastrophic satellite destruction that can actually happen.' (Kessler-syndrome endorsement)
status_reason: Collisional cascading (Kessler syndrome) is a real risk, highlighted by the 2009 Iridium-Cosmos collision and 2021 Russian ASAT test, but it unfolds over years and decades, not within one orbit as shown.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: BB-8, a rolling spherical droid, travels smoothly across desert sand.
critique: Tweet: 'BB-8, a smooth rolling metal spherical ball, would have skidded uncontrollably on sand.'
status_reason: A smooth ball-drive has poor traction on loose sand, but the real BB-8 prop (and Sphero toy) roll on sand using an internal drive with grippy surface; the problem is traction design, not impossibility.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: TIE fighters scream audibly in space battles.
critique: Tweet: 'the TIE fighters made exactly the same sound in the vacuum of space as in planetary atmospheres.'
status_reason: Sound requires a medium; there is no propagation through vacuum.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Han Solo repeats the boast that the Millennium Falcon made the Kessel Run in under 12 parsecs.
critique: Tweets: 'repeats the Millennium Falcon boast of completing the Kessel Run in under 12 parsecs' - 'A Parsec is ... a unit of distance ... equal to 3.26 Light Years. Neither has anything to do with time.'
status_reason: A parsec is indeed a distance (3.26 ly), but the franchise later (Solo, 2018) framed the boast as a shorter route, so a distance claim is not physically absurd.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Starkiller Base drains its star's energy into the planet to power a superweapon.
critique: Tweet: 'if you were to suck all of a star's energy into your planet, your planet would vaporize.'
status_reason: A star's output (~1e26 W for a Sun-like star, total ~1e44 J) vastly exceeds the ~1e32 J gravitational binding energy of an Earth-like planet.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Thor's hammer Mjolnir, said in Marvel lore to be forged in the heart of a dying star, is wielded one-handed.
critique: Tweet: 'If Thor's hammer is made of neutron-star matter, implied by legend, then it weighs as much as a herd of 300-billion elephants.'
status_reason: The density arithmetic (~1e15 kg for a hammer-sized volume of ~4e17 kg/m^3 matter) is right, but canon makes Mjolnir of fictional Uru, and neutron-degenerate matter cannot stay compressed outside a neutron star anyway.

credentials: PhD astrophysics (Columbia, 1991); Frederick P. Rose Director, Hayden Planetarium, American Museum of Natural History
depiction: Superman views the location of his home planet Krypton; the comic places Krypton around a real star chosen by Tyson.
critique: Tyson selected the red dwarf LHS 2520 in Corvus, stated as 27.1 light-years away, as Krypton's sun - a red star 'cooler and smaller than our sun', consistent with the red-sun Superman lore.
status_reason: Gaia parallax (81.57 mas) puts LHS 2520 at ~40 light-years, not 27.1.
